clinicalPearls: A subset of intermediate uveitis defined by snowbanking over the pars plana in the absence of an identifiable systemic infective or inflammatory cause
Characteristically affects children and young adults and is commonly bilateral
Presents with floaters and painless blurring of vision in a quiet-looking eye
Snowballs in the inferior vitreous and a confluent snowbank over the inferior pars plana and ora serrata are typical
Cystoid macular oedema is the chief cause of reduced vision
Neovascularisation of the snowbank may develop and cause vitreous haemorrhage
There is a recognised association with multiple sclerosis, and treatment follows a stepladder of corticosteroids and immunosuppression aimed at controlling macular oedema
reference.pathophysiology: Pars planitis is an idiopathic, chronic, T-cell mediated inflammation of the pars plana and peripheral retina. Organised inflammatory exudate accumulates as a snowbank over the inferior pars plana and ora serrata, while cellular aggregates form snowballs in the vitreous. Persistent inflammation and breakdown of the blood-retinal barrier drive cystoid macular oedema and occasionally peripheral retinal neovascularisation. The condition overlaps with the demyelinating spectrum, hence its association with multiple sclerosis.
additionalInvestigations: Indirect ophthalmoscopy with scleral indentation to demonstrate the inferior snowbank
Optical coherence tomography of the macula for cystoid macular oedema
Fluorescein angiography to detect peripheral leakage and neovascularisation
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain to assess for demyelination
Infective screen including Lyme, syphilis and tuberculosis testing
Sarcoidosis workup to exclude a secondary cause before labelling the disease idiopathic
redFlags: Refractory cystoid macular oedema threatening central vision
reference.prognosis: The course is typically chronic and relapsing; vision is generally preserved when cystoid macular oedema is controlled, although complications such as cataract, glaucoma and retinal detachment may reduce the final outcome.
pitfalls: Labelling the disease as pars planitis without first excluding sarcoidosis, Lyme disease and tuberculosis
Missing an association with multiple sclerosis
Overlooking peripheral neovascularisation of the snowbank
references: American Academy of Ophthalmology, Basic and Clinical Science Course: Uveitis and Ocular Inflammation
